title: Types Are Explicit
goal: Understand how Rust infers primitive types and why it never converts them automatically.

source.attribution: adapted from Day 1: Types and Values

sections.text: You know numbers and booleans from other languages. In Rust, every integer and float has an exact bit width like `i32` or `f64`.

sections.caption: Bit widths are part of the type name.

sections.text: When you omit the type annotation, Rust infers it from context. Unannotated integer literals default to `i32` and float literals default to `f64`.

sections.caption: Integer literals default to i32 and floats to f64.

sections.text: Rust never implicitly converts primitive types for you. Adding an `i32` to an `f64` or a `u8` is a compile error `E0308`.

sections.code:
let x: i32 = 10;
let y: f64 = x as f64;
sections.caption: Explicit conversion uses the as keyword.

sections.text: Type casting with `as` converts primitive values. Converting user defined types and smart pointers is covered in later decks.

explanation: Understand how Rust infers primitive types and why it never converts them automatically.
